Listen to this article Share InnovateNaija’s winners are building for markets worth billions of dollars, from poultry to fish farming to medical diagnostics. Getting there depends on what happens after the prize money lands. NASENI handed out ₦435.5 million on 7 October across four competitions: InnovateNaija, FutureMakers and its Intra-Agency and Inter-Agency innovation challenges. Of that, ₦150 million went to InnovateNaija’s top three, with ₦100 million, ₦30 million and ₦20 million for first, second and third place. Three Inter-Agency winners shared ₦140 million in development grants, three Intra-Agency winners took ₦22.5 million, and six young FutureMakers finalists shared ₦23 million. Those numbers will make headlines, but the people who designed the programme are clear that prize money is the start of the work. Busola Perez-Folayan, head of the NASENI Innovation Hub, said the aim is to help innovators build solutions that can “survive, grow and reach the market”. Why commercialisation is the hard part The Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Dr Kingsley Tochukwu Udeh, framed commercialisation as the reason the programme exists. Turning research into products, he said, lets innovators “generate revenue from their work while contributing to economic growth”, along with jobs and better livelihoods. He also disclosed that President Tinubu has sent a bill to the National Assembly to create a National Research and Innovation Development Fund, which would give dedicated financing to inventions with commercial potential. The finalists’ own accounts show why such a fund is needed. Zang Luka of Plateau State, whose company Zang Global makes a foot-operated computer mouse and Nigerian-made USB cables, said his product is already on sale but production has not scaled. About 40 per cent of his materials are sourced locally, and the rest are imported. Kemisola Bolarinwa of Ekiti State has a working prototype of EwaDX, a wearable device for early breast cancer detection, but it must pass clinical trials and NAFDAC certification before it can be sold. Each case points to the same gap: equipment, testing, regulatory approval and patient capital. The size of the markets in play The winning innovations are aimed at markets large enough to support real companies. A climate-control system that saves even a small share of birds lost each year, or a pond-monitoring tool that lifts yields on fish farms, is competing for a slice of these markets. The fish deficit alone is a gap that imports currently fill. What it means for the wider economy AfriLabs Director of Programmes Nanko Madu argued that Nigeria’s dependence on imported technology carries a hidden cost. Foreign products, she said, are often not designed for Nigeria’s power supply, climate, languages, or purchasing power. Home-built solutions that fit local conditions can compete on those terms, and every unit made here keeps manufacturing jobs and spending in the country. She also made a point about where that value can come from. Running InnovateNaija across all 36 states and the FCT showed that inventive talent is spread well beyond the Lagos-Abuja corridor, and that the real constraint is “a lack of access and opportunity”. State governments are starting to act on that idea. The governors of Abia, Anambra, Enugu, Plateau and Kaduna matched the ₦2.5 million grants for their state champions, doubling each to ₦5 million. Anambra’s Special Adviser on Innovation and Business Incubation, Chinwe Okoli, said the state has already put about ₦364 million into 111 startups, trained 264,000 people in digital skills, and is developing a 13.7-hectare Solution Innovation District. If the National Research and Innovation Development Fund passes, and if more states follow the matching model, InnovateNaija’s winners will have a clearer route from pilot to profit. That route, more than any single prize, is what will decide whether this year’s awards become next year’s companies.
